segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates the people and held object in the locker room, consistently segmenting the distant person on the left (at 4–5 m, facing right and slightly away from the camera while looking down at their phone rather than at the camera wearer) whose head above the nose and body below the hips are out of view. In frames 1–2, it separates the person in the white jersey on the right (3–5 m away, facing toward the camera and bending down) and two to three nearby people standing 0.5–1.5 m behind them (at 0.4–1.2 m from the camera, facing variably away from or toward the camera), before the distant person and lockers occlude most of the nearby crowd in frames 4–5. Out of reach of both the camera wearer and the distant person is the held smartphone (3–5 m away, positioned right of the distant torso and below head level), which lowers slightly in frame 4 and rises again in frame 5 as another hand touches the distant person's left-side sleeve. Compared to RGB, the masks make it easier to count distinct overlapping individuals in the dim foreground of frame 2, though the map completely omits static structural elements like the distant lockers on the right and the nearby walls. The segmentation is unreliable in several places: it misses the phone entirely in frames 1, 4, and 5, mislabels the phone as a 'bottle' overlapping a 'cell phone' in frame 2, misclassifies the bent-over 'JAMES 10' person's torso as a 'backpack' in frame 3 and misses them completely in frames 4–5, and merges the distant person's hands with the phone or torso.
pose: The body and hand skeleton map tracks joint locations on a black background, showing mostly the distant person's right hand in the lower-right to center-right region (3–5 m from the camera wearer, out of reach of both the camera wearer and the distant person) as it holds and taps the smartphone across all five frames. As the sequence progresses, that magenta hand skeleton shifts from the lower right in frame 1 toward the center in frames 2–3, drops to the bottom edge in frame 4 when the arms lower, and returns to the lower center in frame 5 alongside a second magenta hand skeleton on the lower left (about 3 m away from the first hand) where a hand reaches onto the distant person's arm. In frame 3, a yellow upper-torso rectangle and head keypoints appear in the upper-right quadrant for the person in the white jersey (about 0.5–1.0 m away and 4.0 m behind the distant hands), capturing their forward-bent, downward-facing orientation toward the camera wearer. This map reveals exact finger articulation and hand orientation—such as the splayed fingers hovering over the screen in frames 2–3 and the grasping fingers on the sleeve in frame 5—even when motion blur and skin-on-skin contact make joint positions ambiguous in the RGB frames. However, the pose map is highly unreliable overall: it completely fails to detect the distant person's torso, head, and left hand across all frames (likely due to heavy long-range cropping and occlusion), misses all nearby people in frames 1, 2, and 4, and hallucinates a distorted yellow body skeleton entangled with the distant hands in frame 5.
